newsitem.title: CHINA: Family of jailed China dissident to petition court.
newsitem.headline: Family of jailed China dissident to petition court.

text.p: The family of jailed Chinese dissident Wang Dan is planning to petition a Beijing court to overturn his 11-year jail sentence for plotting to overthrow the government, the former student leader's mother said on Tuesday.
The petition would be a mainly symbolic gesture to legal authorities that last year convicted Wang in a trial lasting just four hours, said his mother Wang Lingyun.
"There is no optimism over the result," she told Reuters in a telephone interview. "This is an expression of our attitude."
Wang's family had already prepared documents for the petition, which they expected to submit to the Beijing Higher People's Court later this month, she said.

"In accordance with the legal system, after Wang Dan's appeal he himself or his family are allowed to submit a petition," said the 61-year-old museum researcher, who helped to defend her son during his trial last year.
"I've written a first draft but I haven't sent it yet," she said. "I need to tidy it up before submitting it to the court."
Chinese legal experts say petitions to overturn verdicts that have already survived an appeal have almost no chance of succeeding in forcing a retrial.
Wang Dan, a leader of 1989 pro-democracy student protests that were crushed by the army with heavy loss of life, was sentenced last October to 11 years in jail for subversion.

Wang's brief trial was one of a series of hammer blows dealt by officials to China's tiny pro-democracy movement, which saw almost all its leading members jailed, detained or driven into exile in 1996.
Overseas human rights activists denounced the trial as a politically orchestrated sham, a charge dismissed by Chinese officials who hailed the proceedings as free and fair.

In November, the Beijing Higher People's Court took just 10 minutes to dismiss the 27-year-old dissident's appeal, prompting angry family members to stage a one-hour sit-down protest outside the court.

Wang had previously spent four years in jail for his role in the 1989 protests in Beijing's Tiananmen Square but emerged from imprisonment unbowed, becoming one of China's most articulate political dissenters until vanishing into detention in May 1995.

His case has been repeatedly raised by visiting Western dignitaries, but Beijing -- which dismisses foreign criticism of its human rights record as interference in its internal affairs -- has shown no readiness to soften its stance.

Relatives say Wang suffers from a range of illnesses, many aggravated by conditions at his draughty prison in China's northeastern Liaoning province, which lacks the medical facilities to deal with anything more than common complaints.

"The northeast is very cold and dry, and the doctors themselves say this makes it hard to treat him," said his mother, who this week made the 10-hour train journey from Beijing to Liaoning's Jinzhou city to visit her son.
"His physical conditions is the same as before, but his mental state is alright," she said after returning to Beijing from a three-hour Lunar New Year reunion with her son.
